lessons.sourceObjective: Say breakfast words clearly and greet a server or barista politely in the morning.
lessons.draftObjective: Greet café staff politely, say your name, and recognize common breakfast words in hiragana and katakana.
lessons.sourceFocus: The five vowels, ch, j, ll, rr, silent h and the written accent; morning greetings
lessons.draftFocus: おはようございます is a polite morning greeting. は in わたしは is pronounced wa; です makes a polite statement. Long vowels matter in コーヒー. Katakana often marks loanwords such as コーヒー and メニュー.
sourceCardEnglish: My name is Sam, nice to meet you.
Thank you very much, see you tomorrow!
sourceReaderEnglish: Sam greets the barista Rosa in Oaxaca: Good morning!
Rosa: Hi, how are you?
Sam: My name is Sam, nice to meet you.
Sam reads the menu and orders an orange juice.
Sam also orders a coffee with milk.
Sam doesn't put sugar in the coffee.
To eat, Sam orders eggs with tortillas.
Rosa recommends a churro and sweet bread.
Sam: Thank you very much, see you tomorrow!
draftReaderEnglish: Do you have coffee and bread?
lessons.disposition: original Japanese scene; source objective pinned, card/Reader semantics need qualified comparison

lessons.sourceObjective: Use numbers, prices in pesos, clock times and café quantities to order and check a total.
lessons.draftObjective: Order two coffees and three pieces of bread using Japanese counters, then confirm a price in yen.
lessons.sourceFocus: Numbers 0 to 1,000, prices in pesos, clock time, and café quantities like cups and pieces
lessons.draftFocus: Use コーヒーを二はい for two cups and パンを三つ for three general pieces. ですか asks for confirmation. 円 means yen; café prices vary, so the example total is fictional. The Spanish source's pesos are intentionally adapted to yen.
sourceReaderEnglish: Emma walks into Café Luna in the morning.
Emma looks at the time: It's half past 8.
Luis: There are servings of chilaquiles until noon.
Emma: 2 americanos, please.
Luis: The cup costs 30 pesos and the glass 35.
Emma: In a cup, and 3 pieces of sweet bread.
Luis: The piece costs 20 pesos and the dozen 200.
Emma: Is it 120 pesos?
Luis: Yes, and the slice of cake costs 45.
draftReaderEnglish: Good morning. What would you like to order?
lessons.disposition: original Japanese scene; source objective pinned, card/Reader semantics need qualified comparison

lessons.sourceObjective: Describe food, drinks and tables at a café with ser and estar.
lessons.draftObjective: Ask whether a table is available and describe the temperature or taste of a drink or food without importing Spanish ser/estar grammar.
lessons.sourceFocus: ser for what food is like or where it is from; estar for its condition or a table's status
lessons.draftFocus: Use この席は空いていますか to ask about seat availability. あつい describes a hot drink; つめたい describes a cold one. Japanese adjectives do not map onto the Spanish ser/estar distinction, so this lesson teaches predicate adjectives and current-state expressions instead.
sourceReaderEnglish: Daniel is at a café in Oaxaca, and many tables are taken.
Daniel asks the server: Is this table free?
The server, Rosa, says: Yes, it is free.
Daniel: Is the bread from today?
Rosa: Yes, the sweet bread is fresh.
Daniel: I'm ready to order.
Rosa brings coffee, orange juice and chilaquiles with salsa.
Daniel: The coffee is very hot, but the juice is cold.
Daniel: The salsa is very spicy, but it is delicious.
draftReaderEnglish: Excuse me. Is this seat available?
Yes, it is available. Please go ahead.
This coffee is hot, isn't it?
lessons.disposition: original Japanese scene; source objective pinned, card/Reader semantics need qualified comparison

lessons.sourceObjective: Say what you have, need and want at breakfast, and ask what the café has.
lessons.draftObjective: Say you are hungry, ask whether orange juice is available, and request a fork and napkin politely.
lessons.sourceFocus: tener, hay, necesitar, querer and hay que + infinitive
lessons.draftFocus: ありますか asks whether an item is available. ほしいです expresses what you want; ～をください requests an item politely. Japanese does not copy Spanish tener/hay/querer conjugations. 「新鮮」 is not used to claim juice quality; ask whether it is freshly squeezed if that distinction matters.
sourceCardEnglish: Do you have fresh orange juice?
I'd like a tea without sugar.
Do you have to pay at the register?
sourceReaderEnglish: In a café in Oaxaca, Emma tells the server Luis: I'm very hungry.
Emma: Do you have fresh orange juice?
Luis: Yes, and there is also fresh fruit with breakfast.
Emma: Is there toast?
Luis: Yes, the toast comes with butter and jam.
Emma: I'd like a tea without sugar and a spoon, please.
Emma: I also need a fork and a napkin, please.
Luis: Sure, and you have to pay at the register at the end.
draftReaderEnglish: What would you like to order?
No, it is not freshly squeezed.
A fork and napkin too, please.
lessons.disposition: original Japanese scene; source objective pinned, card/Reader semantics need qualified comparison

lessons.sourceObjective: Say where you are going for breakfast, what you will order, and what you can do at a café.
lessons.draftObjective: Say you plan to eat here and ask whether you may sit outside and pay by card.
lessons.sourceFocus: ir, ir a + infinitive for plans, hacer, and poder for asking permission
lessons.draftFocus: ここで食べます states where an action takes place. ～てもいいですか asks permission. カードで払えますか asks whether card payment is possible. A terrace or payment method is never assumed available.
sourceCardEnglish: I'm going to order the chilaquiles.
We're going to have breakfast here.
Can I sit on the terrace?
Do you make eggs to order?
sourceReaderEnglish: Emma is going to have breakfast at a café near the market.
At the counter, Diego the barista makes coffee.
Emma: I'm going to order the chilaquiles.
Emma: It's for here, not to go.
Emma: Can I sit on the terrace?
Diego: Yes, you can, and the restroom is in the back.
Emma: Can I pay by card?
Diego: Yes, you can pay at the register.
Afterward, Emma is going to go to the bakery for bread.
draftReaderEnglish: Yes, you can pay at the register.

lessons.sourceObjective: Talk about what you eat and drink for breakfast using present-tense verbs.
lessons.draftObjective: Tell another guest what you usually eat and drink, and ask about their breakfast.
lessons.sourceFocus: Present tense of regular -ar, -er and -ir verbs: yo, tú, usted, nosotros, ellos
lessons.draftFocus: Japanese polite nonpast ～ます covers habits and future context; it does not inflect by person like Spanish present-tense verbs. いつも means usually; 毎朝 means every morning. を marks what is eaten or drunk. Avoid assuming another guest lives locally.
sourceCardEnglish: I have breakfast at 8 every day.
Do you drink coffee or tea?
sourceReaderEnglish: Emma has chilaquiles with green salsa for breakfast at her hotel.
Emma: I have breakfast at 8 every day.
Emma puts cheese and avocado on her chilaquiles.
Lucía, another hotel guest, eats scrambled eggs with ham.
Emma: Do you drink coffee or tea?
Lucía: I drink coffee, and my kids eat oatmeal.
Emma: Do you live here in Oaxaca?
Lucía: No, I live in Puebla, and there we eat beans.
Lucía: At home, my husband eats fried eggs with bacon.
draftReaderEnglish: What do you eat for breakfast?
I usually eat bread and eggs.
Which do you drink, coffee or tea?
lessons.disposition: original Japanese scene; source objective pinned, card/Reader semantics need qualified comparison

lessons.sourceObjective: Ask a server or hotel host the basic questions you need at breakfast.
lessons.draftObjective: Ask what breakfast costs, where a restroom is, and what a bread item is called.
lessons.sourceFocus: Question words: qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, cómo, por qué, cuál
lessons.draftFocus: Use 何 (what), どこ (where), いつ (when), いくら (how much), and どれ (which). The question marker か closes a polite question. Ask the host for the actual price rather than assuming breakfast is included.
sourceReaderEnglish: At the hotel, Emma and Tom ask: Who is serving us?
Rosa: I am serving you, what coffee do you want?
Tom: Which is the house coffee?
Rosa: It is the café de olla, why don't you try it?
Emma: How much is the breakfast and when does it end?
Rosa: It is the included breakfast and it ends at 11.
Tom points at the sweet bread: What is this bread called?
Emma: Where is the restroom?
Rosa: It is called a concha, and the restroom is on the right.
draftReaderEnglish: Good morning. How much is breakfast?
I will check your room plan.
For this plan, breakfast is one thousand yen.
Thank you. Where is the restroom?
It is anpan, a sweet bean bun.

lessons.sourceObjective: Say what you don't eat, say you are not ready yet, and ask for more, less or another.
lessons.draftObjective: Say you are not ready, explain that you do not eat meat, and ask for another drink with less sugar.
lessons.sourceFocus: Negatives no, nunca, nadie, nada, todavía no, and amounts with más, menos and otro
lessons.draftFocus: まだ means not yet when paired with a negative. 肉を食べません states that you do not eat meat, and 砂糖は少なめで asks for less sugar. もっと, 少なめ and 別の ask for more, less and another option.
sourceCardEnglish: I never eat peanuts, I'm allergic.
More milk and less sugar, please.
I don't want anything else, thanks.
sourceReaderEnglish: Emma and Tom are having breakfast at a café in Oaxaca.
The server Luis asks: Are you ready?
Emma: We're not ready yet.
Emma: I don't eat meat and Tom doesn't eat dairy products.
Tom: I never eat peanuts, I'm allergic.
Luis: I'm going to ask the kitchen if they use nuts or peanuts.
Luis: The green chilaquiles without cream or cheese have no meat or dairy.
Luis: The corn tortillas don't have gluten.
Emma: Another coffee with more lactose-free milk and less sugar, please.
draftReaderEnglish: Have you decided what to order?
I have not decided yet. Please wait a moment.
I do not eat meat. Do you have a dish without meat?
I will check. Please wait a moment.
lessons.disposition: original Japanese scene; source objective pinned, card/Reader semantics need qualified comparison

lessons.sourceObjective: Ask a server politely for the bill, water or the check, and give simple usted commands.
lessons.draftObjective: Request water and the bill politely, then confirm the accepted way to pay.
lessons.sourceFocus: Polite requests with ¿Puede...? and ¿Me puede...?, and usted commands like tráigame
lessons.draftFocus: ～をください is a direct polite request; ～をいただけますか softens it. お会計 is the bill/payment. Do not translate Spanish usted commands mechanically. Tipping and change practices vary by place, so verify before offering to leave change.
sourceCardEnglish: Could you bring me the bill, please?
Can you give me a glass of water?
sourceReaderEnglish: Anna eats eggs and coffee for breakfast at a café in Oaxaca.
Anna: Can you give me a glass of water?
Luis, the server, brings water with ice and a straw.
Anna: Can you bring me the salt, please?
Anna: Please bring me more cream.
Anna: Could you bring me the bill, please?
Luis: Are you going to pay by card or in cash?
Anna: In cash, here are 200 pesos.
Anna: Keep the change as a tip.
draftReaderEnglish: Excuse me. Could I have a glass of water?
Yes, you can pay by card.
Then I will pay by card.

lessons.sourceObjective: Spot Spanish words you already know and use survival phrases when you don't understand.
lessons.draftObjective: Recognize common katakana loanwords and ask a café worker to repeat or explain an unfamiliar dish.
lessons.sourceFocus: Cognates ending in -ción, -dad and -ente, plus survival phrases for getting help
lessons.draftFocus: Japanese does not have Spanish -ción/-dad cognate patterns. Familiar-looking katakana words such as メニュー and レストラン can help, but meaning and pronunciation still need checking. ゆっくり話してください asks someone to speak slowly; もう一度お願いします asks for repetition.
sourceCardEnglish: Can you speak more slowly, please?
How do you say this in Spanish?
sourceReaderEnglish: Emma has a reservation at 9 at Café Luna.
On the wall there is emergency information in English and Spanish.
Rosa: Today's specialty is different: chilaquiles with chicken.
Emma: Excuse me, I don't understand.
Emma: Can you speak more slowly, please?
Emma: What are the ingredients?
Rosa: The ingredients are tortillas, green salsa, chicken and cheese.
Emma: Is there a vegetarian option?
Rosa: Yes, the vegetarian option is excellent and has a variety of vegetables.
draftReaderEnglish: Excuse me, I do not quite understand.
Yes. It is a seasonal bread.
I will check with the kitchen.
